hook_text: Why are eggs in grey pulp, meal in a sack and syrup in brown glass? Because the product designs the package.
clip_script: Walk the shelves of a spaza shop. Eggs in a grey pulp tray. Maize meal in a woven sack. Cough syrup in brown glass inside a carton. Chips in a puffed-up foil bag. Each package is different because each product is different. Packaging has five jobs: protect, contain, inform, make it convenient, and sell it. The product decides which jobs matter. An egg cracks from a knock, so each one sits in its own cup, held at its strong ends, apart from its neighbours, in pulp that cushions. Meal is heavy and loose, so a strong sack that breathes. Syrup spoils in light and must be kept from children, so brown glass, a child cap, a printed carton. Chips snap and go stale in air, so a sealed bag of nitrogen in foil-lined film. Then match the material: card for stiff and dry, film for waterproof, glass for a total barrier, pulp to cushion. The product is the brief. Read it first.
visual_style: Whiteboard spaza shelf with five products; each is picked up, its top needs listed in two words, and its package drawn around it with the material labelled.
pacing: Shelf tour, five jobs, four products designed in turn, material rule to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and list the three most important needs of a bar of soap before you design its box.
